newsitem.title: CHINA: HK democracy activist sees "revenge" in 1998 polls.
newsitem.headline: HK democracy activist sees "revenge" in 1998 polls.

text.p: An outspoken member of Hong Kong's scrapped Legislative Council on Wednesday said grass roots voters had vowed to take vengeance next year against pro-China forces and eject them from office.

"I've been walking in the streets these days because I've been thrown out of the council, and people keep coming up to me and say make sure you return next year," Emily Lau told reporters at a protest against arrangements for next year's polls.
"They are saying next year is time for revenge -- those people who take away our rights, take away our elected legislature, they will know, we're going to chuck them out all next year," she said.

Hong Kong's elected legislature was scrapped on July 1 when China resumed sovereignty over the territory, after Beijing said democratic reforms enacted in the final years of British colonial rule violated Hong Kong's constitution.

A provisional council appointed by a China-backed committee is sitting in its place and has already passed controversial laws limiting civil rights, but Beijing and the new Hong Kong government have promised fresh polls in the first half of 1998.
About half of the members from the colonial council serve on the provisional legislature, but Lau along with most of the pro-democracy camp refused to participate.
Lau said next year's polls would be the pro-democracy camp's chance to show the world who has the most support, particularly by winning the 20 seats returned by geographic constituencies.

"If we in the pro-democracy movement can win all 20 seats, which is our goal of course, or even if we can't, at least if we win 18 seats, that should be read by the Hong Kong people and the international community as a total triumph and...as a defeat for the pro-communist and pro-business camp," she said.
Under Hong Kong's complex electoral rules, 20 seats are returned by geographic constituencies, 30 by profession-based functional constituencies, and 10 by an electoral committee.
The new government plans to adopt a proportional representation voting method for the 20 directly-elected seats, abolishing the British-style system used in the 1995 polls.

Analysts and the pro-democracy camp have accused the government of trying to boost the chances of pro-China candidates next year after pro-democracy candidates dominated the geographic constituencies in the last elections.
